463.title: The face grows bright
463.hook: in the company of the holy the face grows bright and filth is washed
463.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of the sangat, the congregation gathered before the Guru Granth Sahib, as the saadh sangat, and many make a point of joining it regularly rather than practicing only alone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seventh salok: God beyond reach, and the wondrous story of the holy. Your line was good company. Did you send that message? Today, the first stanza of ashtpadi seven. Day four hundred sixty-three.

There's an old saying in many languages: tell me who your friends are, and I'll tell you who you are. Parents say a version of it to teenagers. Coaches say it to athletes. Researchers keep finding versions of it, too: people around us shape what we eat, how we spend, even how we feel. We soak up the people we sit with. Guru Arjan says it more than four hundred years ago, and says it as good news. The first stanza of ashtpadi seven begins with a face that changes.
screen: `TELL ME WHO YOUR FRIENDS ARE.` → `WE SOAK UP WHO WE SIT WITH.` → `A FACE THAT CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Today's word is saadh sangat. Saadh, you met yesterday: a holy person. Sangat is company, gathering, the people you're with. Put together: the company of the holy. In Sikh life the word sangat on its own came to mean the congregation, the people sitting together before the Guru Granth Sahib. The stanza opens with two lines. Saadh kai sang mukh oojal hot: in the company of the holy, the face becomes bright. Oojal is bright, clean, radiant. In Punjabi, a bright face is also a way of talking about honor: the opposite of a face blackened with shame. So the line means both: you look lighter, and you can hold your head up. Then: saadhsang mal sagalee khot. In the holy company, all the filth is washed off. Mal is dirt, grime, the kind that builds up without your noticing. Neither line says the holy company scrubs you. It's quieter than that. You sit with good people and some of their brightness rubs off on your face. You spend time where the Name is sung, and the grime you didn't know you were carrying starts to loosen. Company shapes you. The stanza doesn't say this is a matter of rules or effort. It says it the way you'd describe sunlight: sit in it and you warm up. That's why, for Sikhs, going to the sangat matters, not just reading alone. The company is part of the medicine.

segments.voice: The practice is to spend time with someone good today: a call, a walk, a meal, even ten minutes. For now, prepare for it. Picture who that could be. Then sit and imagine you're already beside them. Let your face relax, the forehead, the eyes, the mouth, the way a face does in good company. Notice that relaxing is something your face already knows how to do. If you pray, you can ask to be good company for someone else too. The bell holds the time.
Saadh sangat. The company of the holy, where, the stanza says, the face grows bright and the grime washes off.
Your line: company shapes you. Today, spend time with one good person on purpose, and afterward notice your own face. Day four hundred sixty-three.

464.title: Ego leaves in good company
464.hook: in the holy company ego departs and wisdom comes
464.howItsDone: In the sangat, Sikhs sit together on the floor, without ranked seating, to listen to kirtan and katha; many describe that shared listening as where pride softens.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saadh sangat: in the holy company the face grows bright and the grime washes off. Your line was company shapes you. Today, the same stanza goes deeper, past the face. Day four hundred sixty-four.

Picture a dinner where one guest talks the whole time. Their job, their trip, their opinions. Everyone else nods. Now picture a different table, where the oldest person there mostly listens, asks good questions, and laughs at other people's stories. Something odd happens at that second table. Nobody tries to win. The loud ones get quieter without being told. By dessert, people are saying things they've never said out loud. Nobody fought anybody's ego. It just left the room. Ashtpadi seven's first stanza describes exactly that table.
screen: `ONE GUEST TALKS ALL NIGHT.` → `ANOTHER TABLE, ONE WHO LISTENS.` → `NOBODY FOUGHT THE EGO.`

segments.voice: After the bright face and the washed grime, the stanza continues. Saadh kai sang mitai abhimaan: in the company of the holy, pride is erased. Abhimaan is pride, self-importance, the need to be the one who matters most. Mitai means it's rubbed out, the way chalk disappears from a board. Next line: saadh kai sang pragtai sugiaan. In the holy company, true wisdom shows itself. Sugiaan is good knowing, real understanding. Pragtai means it appears, comes into view, as if it had been there all along, just hidden. And then: in the holy company, God is understood to be near. Notice the order. First pride goes. Then wisdom appears. Then God feels close. Sikh teaching often speaks of haumai, the ego that walls the self off, and here is one way the wall comes down: not by attacking it, but by sitting in a place where it has nothing to do. In good company there's no one to compete with, so pride gets bored and wanders off. That's why the carry says quietly. You won't usually notice the moment. You'll just realize, on the way home, that you didn't need to be right tonight, and that you heard something wise you'd have missed if you were talking. The best seat for wisdom, the stanza suggests, is the listening one.
screen: `ABHIMAAN: PRIDE, RUBBED OUT.` · `SUGIAAN: WISDOM COMES INTO VIEW.` · `THEN GOD IS FELT NEAR.` · `NOTHING FOR PRIDE TO DO.` · then, large: `EGO LEAVES QUIETLY.`

segments.voice: The practice: listen more than you speak. Start now, with the room you're in. Close your eyes and listen. The nearest sound. The farthest. The sound under all the others. You don't need to name them or judge them. Just receive them. Notice how little of you is needed to listen. Later today, in one conversation, try the same thing: let the other person finish, wait a breath, ask one question instead of telling one story. If you pray, you can listen for the Name in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Ego leaves in good company. Saadh kai sang mitai abhimaan: in the holy company pride is rubbed out, and wisdom, sugiaan, comes into view.

465.title: Living ashtpadi 7
465.hook: choose your company as you'd choose food
465.tomorrow: Ashtpadi 8, salok: the one who knows God
465.howItsDone: Many Sikhs make a habit of joining the sangat each week, often on Sundays in the diaspora, and of keeping friends who support their remembrance of the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ego leaves in good company: pride rubbed out, wisdom coming into view. Your line was ego leaves quietly. Did you ask the question before telling the story? Today, we live ashtpadi seven. Day four hundred sixty-five.

Most of us think quite hard about food. We read labels. We notice when we've eaten badly for a week and feel sluggish. We know that what goes in becomes, in a fairly literal way, what we are. But company? Mostly it just happens to us. Whoever's at work, whoever's in the group chat, whoever the feed serves up at midnight. We'd never let a vending machine choose all our meals. We often let chance choose all our company. Ashtpadi seven says that company feeds the inner life the way food feeds the body. So it's worth choosing.
screen: `WE READ THE LABELS ON FOOD.` → `COMPANY JUST HAPPENS TO US.` → `IT FEEDS US ALL THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Read through the eight stanzas of ashtpadi seven and the phrase saadh kai sang, in the company of the holy, comes back again and again, each time with something new. The face grows bright. The grime washes off. Pride is rubbed out. Wisdom comes into view. God is felt near. And further on, two lines worth carrying out the door. Saadh kai sang dusman sabh meet: in the holy company, enemies all become friends. Meet, the word for a friend. And: in the holy company, there's no enmity toward anyone. That's a striking claim for a text written in a hard century. Guru Arjan himself was later arrested and executed under the Mughal authorities in Lahore, and Sikhs remember him as the first of their martyr Gurus. The man who wrote these lines knew what enemies were. He still says: in good company, enmity loosens. So what does it mean to live this? Not to drop everyone who isn't saintly. Sikh teaching is clear that the Guru's house is open to all. It means paying attention to where your inner food comes from. Who leaves you lighter, and who leaves you heavier? Where is the Name remembered, and where is it mocked? Then making one small choice toward the lighter table, the way you'd choose a real meal over a bag of chips. Not once in a lifetime. This week.
screen: `SAADH KAI SANG, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `MEET: ENEMIES BECOME FRIENDS.` · `WRITTEN BY A GURU WHO KNEW ENEMIES.` · `ONE SMALL CHOICE, THIS WEEK.` · then, large: `CHOOSE YOUR COMPANY.`

segments.voice: The practice: choose one good company this week. Sit, and let your week ahead appear in your mind, day by day. Where will you be? Who will you see? Now find one gap, an evening, a lunch, a morning walk, and place a good person in it. Or a good place: a gurdwara, a library, a park bench with a wise friend. You're not deciding anything forever. You're choosing one meal. Then sit quietly with that choice, and notice whether it already feels lighter. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi seven. Company feeds the inner life as food feeds the body, and in the holy company, the stanza says, even enemies become friends.
Your line: choose your company. Before today ends, put one good company on your calendar for this week, by name. Day four hundred sixty-five.

466.title: Ashtpadi 8, salok: the one who knows God
466.hook: the salok introduces the God-conscious one
466.howItsDone: Sikhs read ashtpadi eight of Sukhmani Sahib as a portrait of the brahm giaanee, and teachers often use it to describe the qualities a Sikh grows toward rather than a title anyone claims.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi seven: company as food, and enemies becoming friends. Your line was choose your company. Who's on your calendar? Today, ashtpadi eight paints a portrait. Day four hundred sixty-six.

Some of the most famous passages in any scripture are portraits. Not commands, not stories, but a description of a person. Here is what such a person is like. Here's how they walk, how they speak, how they treat a stranger. Portraits work differently from rules. You don't obey a portrait. You look at it, and something in you leans toward it. Ashtpadi seven described the holy company. Ashtpadi eight zooms in on one face in that company and gives it a name. For eight stanzas, Guru Arjan paints the brahm giaanee.
screen: `A SCRIPTURE THAT PAINTS A PERSON.` → `YOU DON'T OBEY A PORTRAIT.` → `ONE FACE, EIGHT STANZAS.`

segments.voice: Brahm giaanee. Brahm here is the Supreme, God beyond all forms. Giaan is knowing; giaanee is the one who knows. So, the one who knows God. Many translators say the God-conscious one, and that's closer, because this knowing isn't information. It's not someone who has read the most books about God. It's someone whose whole awareness is soaked in God, the way a cloth is soaked in dye. The salok gives three marks. First: true in the mind. Second: true in the mouth, so what they say matches what they are, with no gap between the inside and the outside. Third: they see nothing but the One. Not that they stop seeing people or trees or traffic, but that in everything they see, they see the One. And the salok ends: Nanak, these are the marks of the brahm giaanee. The word for marks is lachhan, signs, features, the way you'd describe what makes a face recognizable. That's the key. The salok isn't handing out a title. It's describing features. You'd recognize such a person by these marks, not by their robes or their rank. Over the next stanzas the portrait fills in: a lotus, the earth, the sun, the wind. Sikh teachers often remind their listeners that this is a portrait to grow toward, not a badge to pin on oneself or anyone else. Today, just look at the face.
screen: `BRAHM: GOD. GIAANEE: ONE WHO KNOWS.` · `TRUE IN MIND, TRUE IN MOUTH.` · `SEEING THE ONE IN EVERYTHING.` · `LACHHAN: MARKS, NOT A TITLE.` · then, large: `THE GOD-CONSCIOUS ONE.`

segments.voice: The practice: think of someone wise and gentle. Not famous, necessarily. Someone you've actually met. Picture them. Is there a gap between what they say and who they are? Probably very little; that's part of why you trust them. Notice how they look at people, at a waiter, a child, a stranger. Let their face rest in your mind. You don't need to call them a saint. Just let yourself lean toward what you see. If you pray, you can give thanks that such people exist. The bell holds the time.
Brahm giaanee. The one who knows God, the God-conscious one: true in mind, true in speech, seeing the One in all.
Your line: the god-conscious one. Today, try one small thing from the salok: say only what you mean, once, with no gap between inside and outside. Day four hundred sixty-six.

467.title: Like a lotus in water
467.hook: the God-conscious one lives untouched, like a lotus in water
467.howItsDone: Sikhs often use the lotus in water, from Sukhmani Sahib and Guru Nanak's Sidh Gosht, to describe living as a householder in the world without being stained by it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the brahm giaanee: true in mind, true in speech, seeing the One in all. Your line was the god-conscious one. Today, the portrait gets its first picture. Day four hundred sixty-seven.

If you've ever seen a lotus up close, you'll know the trick. It grows from the mud at the bottom of a pond. Its stem rises through murky water. And then the leaf and the flower open on the surface, and if you splash water on them, it beads up and rolls right off. The leaf is in the water its whole life, and it doesn't get wet. Poets across India have loved this flower for thousands of years, and the Guru Granth Sahib uses it too. Today it opens the very first stanza of the brahm giaanee's portrait.
screen: `ROOTED IN MUD.` → `RISING THROUGH MURKY WATER.` → `THE WATER BEADS AND ROLLS OFF.`

segments.voice: The first line: brahm giaanee sadaa nirlep. The God-conscious one is always nirlep, untouched, unstained. Lep is a coating, a smear, something that sticks to you. Nir means without. So: nothing sticks. Then the picture: jaise jal meh kamal alep. Just as the lotus in water stays unstained. Kamal is the lotus. Notice what the picture doesn't say. It doesn't say the lotus leaves the pond. It doesn't float off to some clean place. It lives in the water, all its life. That matters in Sikh teaching, which asks people to live in the world, work, marry, raise children, pay bills, and not run away to the forest. Guru Nanak used the same image when wandering yogis asked him how to cross the world: like a lotus in water, untouched, and like a duck swimming in a stream, whose feathers stay dry. The brahm giaanee is in the mess. The mess just doesn't stick. The very next line adds a second picture: the God-conscious one is free of fault, like the sun that dries up everything. The sun shines on clean and dirty places alike, and it doesn't get dirty doing it. Two pictures, one idea. You can be fully in the middle of things, the office, the family argument, the crowded train, and still not be stained by them. Untouched doesn't mean unfeeling. It means the anger in the room doesn't become your anger.
screen: `NIRLEP: NOTHING STICKS.` · `KAMAL: THE LOTUS STAYS IN THE POND.` · `GURU NANAK: THE LOTUS AND THE DUCK.` · `THE SUN, UNSTAINED BY WHAT IT DRIES.` · then, large: `UNTOUCHED, LIKE THE LOTUS.`

segments.voice: The practice: stay calm in one mess. First, rehearse it now. Think of a small mess waiting for you today: an inbox, a difficult relative, a sink full of dishes. Picture yourself in the middle of it. Then picture the lotus leaf, and the water beading up and rolling off. Breathe in: I'm in the water. Breathe out: it rolls off. You're not pretending the mess isn't there. You're just not letting it soak in. Then, later today, try it for real, once. The bell holds the time.
Like a lotus in water. Jaise jal meh kamal alep: the God-conscious one lives in the world, untouched, like the lotus in the pond.
screen: `LIKE A LOTUS IN WATER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: untouched, like the lotus. In one mess today, stay in it, do your part, and let what isn't yours roll off. Day four hundred sixty-seven.

468.title: Like the earth
468.hook: the God-conscious one is like the earth, dug by some, anointed by others, the same to both
468.howItsDone: Sikhs read this stanza of Sukhmani Sahib as a picture of steady, equal treatment of everyone, an ideal also lived in the gurdwara, where all sit and eat together as equals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, like a lotus in water: in the pond all its life, and the water rolls off. Your line: untouched, like the lotus. Did anything roll off today? The same stanza has two more pictures. Day four hundred sixty-eight.

Stand in a field and think about what the ground under your feet puts up with. A farmer drives a plow through it. Someone digs a well, a grave, a foundation. Someone else kneels and plants a rose, or pours fragrant oil on it at a shrine. Rain pounds it. Children run on it. And through all of it, the earth does the same thing it always does. It holds everything up, and it grows whatever is put into it. It doesn't sulk at the plow or preen at the perfume. Guru Arjan saw a portrait of a person in that.
screen: `A PLOW, A WELL, A GRAVE.` → `A ROSE, FRAGRANT OIL.` → `THE EARTH DOES THE SAME THING.`

segments.voice: The first stanza of ashtpadi eight keeps painting. After the lotus and the sun, a third picture: the brahm giaanee looks on all alike, as the wind blows the same on king and beggar. Raaj is the king, rank the poorest of the poor. The wind doesn't check who it's touching. Then the fourth: brahm giaanee kai dheeraj ek. The God-conscious one has one, steady patience, jio basudhaa, like the earth. Basudhaa is an old word for the earth, literally the one who holds treasure. Kooo khodai, kooo chandan lep: one person digs it, another anoints it with sandalwood paste. And the earth is the same to both. Sandalwood paste is what you'd smear on something precious, something honored. So the picture is as extreme as it can be: one person tears into you, another honors you, and you don't change. Notice it's not saying the earth doesn't notice the plow. It's saying the earth doesn't become a different earth depending on who's standing on it. That's dheeraj, patience, steadiness. The stanza closes with a last picture: this is the brahm giaanee's quality, the way it is fire's natural nature to burn. Not forced. Just what fire is. Lotus, sun, wind, earth, fire. Every picture in this stanza is nature, doing what it does, the same for everyone. And every one is a way of saying: equal treatment, flowing from who you are, not from who's in front of you.
screen: `THE WIND ON KING AND BEGGAR.` · `BASUDHAA: THE EARTH THAT HOLDS.` · `ONE DIGS, ONE ANOINTS.` · `STEADY, LIKE FIRE'S NATURE.` · then, large: `LIKE THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: The practice: treat two people the same. Think of two people you'll meet today, one who usually treats you well and one who doesn't. Picture each in turn. Notice how your body changes: maybe you open up for one and brace for the other. Now picture yourself as the ground under both of them. Steady. Holding. The same. Breathe in, feeling your weight on the floor. Breathe out, letting both faces rest on you equally. Later, give them both the same greeting. The bell holds the time.
Like the earth. Jio basudhaa: dug by one, anointed with sandalwood by another, and the same to both.
Your line: like the earth. Today, greet the person who's hardest for you exactly the way you'd greet the easiest. Day four hundred sixty-eight.

469.title: Living ashtpadi 8
469.hook: the brahm giaanee is a portrait to grow into, not a title to claim
469.howItsDone: Sikhs read ashtpadi eight of Sukhmani Sahib as a portrait of qualities to cultivate, and many teachers caution against anyone claiming the title brahm giaanee for themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, like the earth: dug by one, anointed by another, the same to both. Your line was like the earth. Today, we live ashtpadi eight. Day four hundred sixty-nine, the end of a week.

A child puts on her father's shoes and clomps around the kitchen. They're enormous. She trips. Everyone laughs, and nobody thinks she's pretending to be him. She's trying them on. She's leaning toward a size she'll grow into one day. There's a world of difference between that child and someone who buys a uniform and starts giving orders. One is growing. The other is claiming. Ashtpadi eight's portrait of the brahm giaanee can be worn either way. Sikh teachers have long warned which way not to wear it.
screen: `A CHILD IN HER FATHER'S SHOES.` → `TRYING ON, NOT PRETENDING.` → `GROWING, OR CLAIMING?`

segments.voice: Ashtpadi eight paints its portrait for eight stanzas. True in mind and mouth. A lotus in water. The sun, the wind, the earth, the fire. And more: the God-conscious one is filled with humility, gareebee, the word that also means being poor, low, unassuming. The God-conscious one delights in doing good for others. Friend and enemy look the same to them. And then, deep in the ashtpadi, a line that stops the whole thing becoming a checklist: only a brahm giaanee knows the state of a brahm giaanee. In other words, you can't assess it from outside, and you certainly can't award it to yourself. Put the humility and that line together, and a quiet logic appears. Anyone who announces I am a brahm giaanee has just shown a lack of the very first quality in the portrait. That's why Sikh teachers often say: read ashtpadi eight as a mirror and a direction, never as a label. Living it means picking one quality, the earth's patience, the lotus's dryness, the wind's fairness, and growing into it, a little, the way a child grows into shoes. And this is where the week ends. Seven days ago, the holy company: the face growing bright, ego leaving quietly, and company chosen like food. Then the brahm giaanee: true inside and out, a lotus, and the earth. A week of good people. One portrait to grow toward.
screen: `GAREEBEE: HUMILITY, LOWLINESS.` · `ONLY THEY KNOW THAT STATE.` · `TO CLAIM IT IS TO LACK IT.` · `ONE QUALITY, A LITTLE AT A TIME.` · then, large: `GROW INTO IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: practice one quality from the portrait. Pick one. The lotus: in the mess, untouched. The earth: the same to the one who digs and the one who honors. The wind: fair to king and beggar. Gareebee: humble, low, unassuming. Don't pick the hardest. Pick the one that feels like a shoe slightly too big. Hold it in mind. Breathe in its name. Breathe out, and picture one moment today where you could try it on. If you pray, you can ask for help to grow. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi eight. The brahm giaanee is a portrait to grow into, with humility at its heart, never a title to claim.
Your line: grow into it. Today, try on your one quality once, and tell no one you're doing it. Day four hundred sixty-nine. A week, done.
